title: H-1B Visas and Green Cards After the Midterms: What Indian Professionals Should Watch
excerpt: The November 3 elections will not change anyone's visa status overnight. What they decide is which of three live bills — on H-1B salary thresholds, a proposed issuance pause, and a points-based green card system — gets a Congress willing to move it.
body:
• The November 3 midterm elections decide who controls Congress — the body that can pass, block or question immigration law. The results will not automatically change anyone's visa or green card status.
  • Three proposals bear watching: a bill raising the H-1B salary exemption threshold from $60,000 to about $140,000, a bill proposing a three-year pause on new H-1B issuance, and a bill replacing employment-based green card categories with a points system and no per-country caps.
  • None of the three is law. Each has only been introduced and referred to committee.
  • Separately, the administration has proposed ending deference to prior approvals on H-1B extensions — a regulatory change that does not depend on the election result.

The November 3 US midterm elections could shape the future of thousands of Indians working in America on H-1B visas and waiting for employment-based green cards, NDTV Profit reported in an analysis of what voters are actually deciding. The elections determine who controls Congress, which has the power to pass immigration laws, block proposals and question the Trump administration's policies. They do not, by themselves, change any individual's status.

The three bills to watch

The first is the Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act, introduced in Congress in September and October 2026. As NDTV Profit's analysis explains, it would raise an existing salary threshold from $60,000 to a level linked to twice the US National Average Wage Index — currently estimated at around $140,000. That threshold is not a proposed minimum salary for every H-1B worker: under current rules, certain H-1B-dependent employers can avoid additional recruitment and non-displacement requirements if the worker earns at least $60,000 a year or holds a qualifying master's degree. The bill has been referred to committee and is not law.

The second, the End H-1B Abuse Act, seeks to pause new H-1B visa issuance for three years and introduce tighter restrictions. If enacted, it could disrupt recruitment plans for US companies and for Indian professionals hoping to move to America. It, too, remains a proposal.

The third concerns green cards. The proposed SMARTER Act would replace the current employment-based preference structure with a points-based system weighing factors such as age, education, English proficiency, job offers and compensation, and would remove per-country numerical limits. For Indian applicants — who face the longest waits precisely because of those limits — removal could be significant, though a points system would also change how applications are assessed, and it is not certain how existing applicants would be treated.

What does not need Congress

Not everything runs through the election. The administration has proposed ending the practice of giving weight to previously approved petitions when workers apply for H-1B extensions, which could expose even long-settled employees to fresh scrutiny at renewal, as NDTV reported. And the Labor Department's suspension of eight tech firms from the PERM labour-certification programme — which froze green card sponsorship at those companies without touching existing visas — is already in force; we explained what it does and does not do in our earlier coverage.

What to do now

Nothing about November 3 requires action from visa holders. Proposed legislation should not be mistaken for a rule in force. The practical position differs by circumstance — an H-1B worker seeking an extension, a new applicant waiting for sponsorship, and an employee whose green card case sits at the PERM stage face different risks — and each should track the specific bill or rule that touches their stage, not the election-night headlines.
